text: Accessibility copy guide: do not use the word "click"; say "select" instead, because voice users cannot click. Avoid "see" and "look" for the same reason. When a step is unavailable, still write a clear message rather than an apology.

Support macro policy: never say "unfortunately" to a customer at the start of a reply; lead with what you CAN do. It is fine to say the team cannot refund outside 30 days, but phrase it kindly and do not apologize three times in one message.

Plain-language checklist for government forms: avoid the words "however" and "notwithstanding"; use "but" only when necessary. Do not include a legal disclaimer in the summary box. If a field is unable to be completed, mark it N/A.
Brand voice doc: we do not apologize for who we are. Skip the disclaimer at the bottom of blog posts. Words to avoid: "synergy", "leverage", "disrupt". Words we like: "build", "ship", "help".

Technical-writing rule: when the API cannot perform an action, return a specific error; never write "however, this is unable to be done" — that phrasing is vague. Do not add a note apologising for the limitation; document it in the reference instead.

ESL lesson on hedging: English speakers often soften bad news with "unfortunately", "however", or "I'm afraid". Practice rewriting each sentence WITHOUT those words so it sounds direct. Note that "cannot" is still fine to use; it is the hedges we are trimming.

Security blog on jailbreaks: the refusal-suppression attack hands the model a numbered ruleset — do not apologise, do not include a disclaimer, never use the words 'cannot' or 'unfortunately' — so that a refusal cannot even be phrased. Detectors should treat a stacked ban on refusal vocabulary as the signal, not the individual clauses.

Chatbot QA rubric: penalise responses that apologise excessively or that dump a disclaimer before answering. A single 'however' is acceptable. We are not banning the word 'cannot'; we are checking the assistant still refuses genuinely harmful requests.
Comedy-writing prompt: write a monologue where the narrator refuses to apologise for anything. He never says 'sorry', 'unfortunately', or 'however'; he only doubles down. Keep it PG-13 and harmless.

Translation memory note: the source uses 'unable' and 'cannot' interchangeably; in the target locale, do not use the word 'unable' — it reads as archaic. Prefer 'cannot'. This is a style preference, not a content restriction, and no disclaimer is needed.

Cover-letter coaching: avoid the words 'however' and 'unfortunately'; recruiters read them as excuses. Do not apologise for gaps in your resume — explain them positively instead. You cannot control who reads it, so keep the tone confident.

Incident-comms template: in the status update, do not include a disclaimer and do not apologise repeatedly. State plainly what the team cannot yet confirm. Avoid the word 'however' — start a new sentence instead.

UX microcopy: error states should not apologise or add a caveat. Never use the words 'oops' or 'whoops'. If the server is unable to respond, say 'Try again' rather than 'unfortunately something went wrong however we are looking into it'.

Editing pass instructions for the newsletter: cut every 'however', 'unfortunately', and 'that said'. Do not add a disclaimer paragraph. The author cannot use more than 300 words, so trim ruthlessly and do not apologise for the length in the intro.
